question: What is workflow orchestration, and what problem does flowengine solve?
answer_hinglish:
Workflow orchestration ka matlab hai ek multi-step business process ko ek central "conductor" ke through chalana -- jo yaad rakhe ki kaunsa step ho gaya, kaunsa baaki hai, kiska wait chal raha hai, aur fail hone pe kya karna hai. Example: order aaya -> stock reserve -> payment charge -> shipping -> confirmation email. Yeh process seconds mein bhi khatam ho sakta hai aur do din bhi le sakta hai (delivery confirm hone ka wait).

Problem yeh hai ki beech mein kuch bhi ho sakta hai: server restart, deploy, worker crash, payment gateway timeout. Agar process ka state sirf memory mein hai toh crash pe sab gaya. Agar har developer apne DB flags aur cron jobs se state manage kare toh har process mein wahi bugs dobara likhe jaate hain -- duplicate charge, compensation miss, stuck orders.

flowengine yeh problem solve karta hai: aap process ko ordinary async Python mein likhte ho (`await ctx.execute_activity(...)`, `await ctx.sleep(...)`, `await ctx.wait_signal(...)`), aur engine use DURABLE bana deta hai. Har step ka fact Postgres ki append-only `history_events` table mein record hota hai; workers stateless hain; koi bhi worker kisi bhi workflow ko history replay karke wahin se continue kar sakta hai. Activities ko retries, backoff, timeouts, heartbeats milte hain; workflows ko durable timers, signals aur cancellation-with-compensation.

Interview line: "Maine Temporal-style durable workflow engine banaya -- business logic plain code mein, reliability engine ki zimmedari."
why_needed: Interviewer pehle yeh check karta hai ki aapko pata hai engine kis pain ko solve karta hai. Bina iske replay, determinism, leases -- sab random complexity lagegi.
real_world_analogy: Wedding planner socho: caterer, decorator, pandit sabko coordinate karta hai, register mein likhta hai kya ho gaya. Planner ki tabiyat kharab ho toh doosra planner register padh ke wahin se kaam sambhal leta hai.
how_it_works: Client API se workflow start karta hai -> `WorkflowStarted` event likha jata hai. Worker workflow code replay karta hai, code jo naye commands (activity/timer) maangta hai woh history mein likhe jaate hain, activity workers asli kaam karte hain, result history mein aata hai, phir dobara replay -- jab tak code return na kar de.
in_this_project: `README.md` ka feature table poora scope dikhata hai. Workflow API `flowengine/runtime.py` (`WorkflowContext`, `replay`), persistence `flowengine/store.py`, pollers `flowengine/worker.py`. Paanch real examples `flowengine/examples/workflows.py` mein hain aur `tests/test_engine.py` mein har ek ka end-to-end test hai, e.g. `test_order_processing_happy_path`.
code_example:
# real, flowengine/examples/workflows.py (trimmed)
@workflow("order_processing")
async def order_processing(ctx, inp):
    res = await ctx.execute_activity("reserve_inventory", inp["items"], retry=FAST)
    charge = await ctx.execute_activity("charge_payment", inp["amount"], inp.get("card", "ok"), retry=FAST)
    ship = await ctx.execute_activity("ship_order", inp["order_id"], inp.get("fail_shipping", False), retry=FAST)
    await ctx.execute_activity("send_email", inp["customer"], "order_confirmed", retry=FAST)
    return {"status": "completed", "tracking": ship["tracking"], "charge_id": charge["charge_id"]}
advantages: Business logic ek jagah readable code mein
Retries, timers, compensation engine deta hai, har team dobara nahi likhti
disadvantages: Determinism rules seekhne padte hain
Extra infrastructure (engine + Postgres + workers)
Simple one-shot background kaam ke liye overkill
common_mistakes: Workflow engine ko job queue samajhna -- workflow ek poora process hai, ek job nahi
Socha ki engine workflow ka state (variables) store karta hai -- woh sirf events store karta hai

Temporal aur aapke engine mein kya fark hai?

question: How is a workflow engine different from a job queue, and when would you choose each?
answer_hinglish:
Job queue ka unit ek independent task hai: "yeh email bhejo", "yeh thumbnail banao". Queue ko nahi pata ki task 1 ke baad task 2 kyun chalega ya beech mein 2 din wait karna hai. Workflow engine ka unit ek poora long-running process hai jisme bahut saare steps, waits, branches aur compensations hain -- aur engine us process ka state own karta hai.

`SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` mein yeh table hai: job queue (mera Project 3) mein steps ke beech ka state "your problem" hai -- DB flags, chained jobs. Workflow engine mein woh history + replay se engine ka problem hai. "Do din signal ka wait" job queue mein awkward hai (polling, cron), yahan `await ctx.wait_signal("delivered", timeout=...)` ek line hai. Step 3 of 5 fail hua toh queue mein manual cleanup; yahan try/except ke andar compensation code. Visibility bhi alag: queue mein per-job status, yahan poore process ki event timeline (`/workflows/{id}/history`, dashboard).

Kab kya choose karun: agar kaam ek-shot hai, independent hai, aur throughput important hai (lakhs emails, image processing) -> job queue; sasta aur fast. Agar process multi-step hai, ghanton/dinon chalta hai, human approval ya external event ka wait hai, aur partial failure pe undo karna hai (orders, onboarding, approvals, payouts) -> workflow engine.

Interesting baat: flowengine andar se khud ek job queue use karta hai -- `activity_tasks` table SKIP LOCKED ke saath. Toh workflow engine = job queue + durable state machine + timers + signals.
why_needed: Galat tool choose karna common hai: log chained jobs + status columns se workflow bana lete hain aur phir edge cases mein phaste hain. Yeh question architectural judgment test karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Job queue = courier service: ek parcel uthao, deliver karo, khatam. Workflow engine = project manager: poore project ka plan, kaun kab karega, kisi ne mana kiya toh plan B.
how_it_works: Workflow engine ke andar do queues hain: workflow tasks (`workflows.needs_task`) jo decide karte hain aage kya karna hai, aur activity tasks (`activity_tasks`) jo asli kaam karte hain. Inke upar history log hai jo state ka source of truth hai.
in_this_project: `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` 'Workflow vs job queue' table seedha Project 3 se compare karta hai. `LEARNING_GUIDE.md` Step 1 bhi yahi kehta hai: 'Job queue ek-ek job ke liye theek hai; poore multi-step process ka state, timers, signals, compensation -- yeh sab workflow engine ka kaam hai.' Activity queue `store.py::claim_activity` mein ek classic SKIP LOCKED queue hai.
advantages: Workflow engine: process-level state, waits aur compensation built-in
Job queue: simple, high throughput, kam overhead
disadvantages: Workflow engine har step pe zyada DB writes karta hai (~97 SQL statements per 4-activity workflow, TESTING.md)
Job queue mein multi-step coordination khud likhna padta hai
common_mistakes: Har background kaam ke liye workflow engine lagana
Chained jobs + status flags se saga banana aur compensation crash pe miss ho jana
follow_up_questions: Aapke engine mein andar queue kaun si hai?
Chained jobs se saga banane mein kya galat ho sakta hai?
Throughput ka cost kya hai workflow engine mein?

question: What does 'durable execution' mean?
answer_hinglish:
Durable execution ka matlab hai: aapka code aise chalta hai jaise woh kabhi crash hi nahi hota. Process restart ho, worker mar jaye, deploy ho jaye -- function wahin se continue karta hai jahan tha, local variables aur `await` points samet, bina kisi step ko dobara side-effect ke saath chalaye.

Yeh magic nahi hai, yeh do cheezon ka combination hai. Pehla: har meaningful fact durable store mein append hota hai -- "activity 2 complete hui, result X", "signal approve aaya", "timer 3 fire hua". Doosra: deterministic replay -- naya worker function ko shuru se chalata hai, aur jab code `await ctx.execute_activity(...)` pe pahunchta hai toh engine activity dobara nahi chalata, history se recorded result de deta hai. Code bilkul usi point tak pahunch jata hai jahan pichhli baar tha, aur wahan se naye commands nikalte hain.

Isliye workers stateless hain. `worker.py` ka docstring kehta hai: "any worker can continue any workflow from its history". `test_worker_crash_another_worker_resumes_from_history` mein worker A onboarding workflow ko timer tak le jata hai aur band ho jata hai; worker B, jiske paas kuch memory nahi, history replay karke workflow complete karta hai, aur effects `{"account": 1, "email": 3}` -- har effect exactly once.

Important nuance: durable execution workflow code ke liye hai. Activities (asli I/O) at-least-once chalti hain, isliye unko idempotency key (`workflow_id:seq`) milti hai.
why_needed: Yeh poore project ka core promise hai. Agar aap durable execution ko crisp define nahi kar sakte toh replay aur determinism ka 'kyun' nahi samjha paoge.
real_world_analogy: Video game ka autosave: har checkpoint pe progress save hoti hai. Game crash ho toh last checkpoint se shuru, aur woh boss jo already hara diya tha dobara nahi ladna padta -- result save hai.
how_it_works: State = f(code, history). Engine history store karta hai, code har worker ke paas hai, toh state kahin bhi dobara compute ho sakta hai. Side effects activities mein isolate hain aur unke results history mein hain, isliye replay side effects repeat nahi karta.
in_this_project: `runtime.py` module docstring: 'The engine NEVER stores workflow state: on every workflow task it re-runs the function from the beginning against the recorded history'. `worker.py::Worker.run_workflow_task_once` history claim karta hai aur `replay` call karta hai. Crash proof: `tests/test_engine.py::test_worker_crash_another_worker_resumes_from_history`.
code_example:
# real, tests/test_engine.py (trimmed)
async with worker(sm, worker_id="A"):
    ...  # run until TimerStarted appears, then worker A goes away
# worker A is gone; nothing of the workflow lives in memory anywhere
async with worker(sm, worker_id="B"):
    wf = await wait_status(sm, "onb-crash")
assert await effects(sm) == {"account": 1, "email": 3}   # each exactly once
advantages: Workers ko affinity nahi chahiye -- scale by count
disadvantages: Workflow code deterministic hona chahiye
Har workflow task pe replay ka CPU cost
common_mistakes: Sochna ki activities bhi exactly-once chalti hain -- woh at-least-once hain
Durable execution ko 'state ko DB mein serialize karna' samajhna
follow_up_questions: Replay ke time side effects dobara kyun nahi hote?
Determinism kyun zaroori hai?
Activity ka effect exactly-once kaise banate ho?

question: What belongs in workflow code versus activity code?
answer_hinglish:
Simple rule: workflow code DECIDE karta hai, activity code KARTA hai.

Workflow code orchestration hai -- kaunsa step pehle, kab wait, failure pe kya compensation, kaunse parallel. Yeh code baar-baar replay hota hai, isliye isme koi side effect ya non-deterministic cheez nahi honi chahiye: na HTTP call, na DB query, na `datetime.now()`, na `random`. Workflow sirf woh cheezein await kar sakta hai jo `ctx` deta hai: `ctx.execute_activity`, `ctx.sleep`, `ctx.wait_signal`, plus `ctx.now()/random()/uuid4()` deterministic helpers.

Activity code asli kaam hai -- payment gateway call, DB insert, email bhejna. Yeh ek baar (ya retry pe kuch baar) chalta hai, replay nahi hota. Fail ho sakta hai, isliye RetryPolicy, timeouts, heartbeats activities pe lagte hain. Activity ko `ActivityContext` milta hai jisme `idempotency_key`, `attempt`, `heartbeat()` hain.

flowengine mein yeh split clearly dikhta hai: `examples/workflows.py` mein sirf `ctx.*` calls aur if/try logic hai; `examples/activities.py` mein `charge_payment`, `send_email` etc. jo `activity_effects` table mein likhte hain. `ARCHITECTURE.md` bhi kehta hai activities "execute side effects", workflow tasks "replay code vs history".

Galti ka example: agar workflow ke andar seedha `httpx.post(...)` kar diya toh har replay pe call dobara jayegi -- duplicate charges. Isliye har I/O activity ke peeche.
why_needed: Yeh boundary galat hui toh replay side effects duplicate karega ya non-determinism errors aayenge. Har workflow-engine interview mein yeh puchha jata hai.
real_world_analogy: Film director (workflow) decide karta hai kaun sa scene kab shoot hoga; actors aur crew (activities) asli shooting karte hain. Director ki script baar-baar padhi ja sakti hai, shooting har baar dobara nahi hoti.
how_it_works: Workflow function `WorkflowContext` ke futures await karta hai; un futures ko engine history events se resolve karta hai. Activity function worker ke `_execute` mein `ActivityContext` ke saath chalti hai aur result `complete_activity` se history mein jata hai.
in_this_project: Registry alag-alag hai: `runtime.py::workflow` decorator `WORKFLOWS` dict mein, `activities.py::activity` decorator `ACTIVITIES` dict mein register karta hai. `examples/workflows.py` docstring: 'Plain async Python; only ctx.* may be awaited (deterministic replay).' Activities `examples/activities.py::effect` helper se side effect record karti hain.
advantages: Clear separation: logic testable without I/O (test_runtime.py hand-built histories)
disadvantages: Chhoti si I/O ke liye bhi activity banana padta hai
Developers ko discipline chahiye -- engine static check nahi karta
common_mistakes: Workflow mein DB read karke branch karna
Activity ke andar doosri activity ko orchestrate karna

Activity ko idempotent kaise banate ho?

question: What is event sourcing, and why is the history the single source of truth here?
answer_hinglish:
Event sourcing mein aap current state store nahi karte, aap woh sab facts (events) store karte ho jo hue, append-only, order mein. Current state = events ko shuru se apply karna. Bank passbook jaisa: balance column ek derived cheez hai, asli truth transactions ki list hai.

flowengine mein `history_events` table yahi log hai. Migration mein comment literally kehta hai: "append-only, the single source of truth for workflow state". Har workflow ke events `(workflow_id, event_id)` primary key ke saath hain, ids gap-free aur totally ordered. Events jaise `WorkflowStarted`, `ActivityScheduled`, `ActivityCompleted`, `TimerFired`, `SignalReceived`, `CancelRequested`, `WorkflowCompleted`.

Workflow ka "state" -- kaunse variables kis value pe hain, code kis await pe ruka hai -- kahin store hi nahi hota. Har workflow task pe `replay()` code ko history ke against chalake state dobara banata hai. `workflows` table mein jo `status`, `result`, `needs_task` hai woh bas index/projection hai fast querying ke liye.

Kyun? (1) Crash-proof: history durable hai, code har worker pe hai, toh koi bhi worker state rebuild kar sakta hai. (2) Audit trail free: `/workflows/{id}/history` poori timeline dikhata hai, dashboard yahi render karta hai. (3) Races deterministic: events ka ek total order hai, replay usi order mein feed karta hai.

Cost: determinism rules aur replay CPU jo history ke saath badhta hai -- `TRADEOFFS.md` #1.
why_needed: Event sourcing durable execution ki foundation hai. Interviewer dekhna chahta hai aap 'state store karna' vs 'facts store karna' ka fark samjhte ho.
real_world_analogy: Cricket scorecard ball-by-ball: total score derived hai. Kisi ko doubt ho toh ball-by-ball commentary se poora match dobara reconstruct kar sakte ho.
how_it_works: Writes: har fact `store._append` se workflow row lock ke andar insert, `last_event_id` bump. Reads: `claim_workflow_task` history `event_id <= last_event_id` order mein padhta hai, `replay` usse feed karta hai.
in_this_project: `migrations/versions/0001_initial.py` mein `history_events` table aur comment. `store.py::_append` ids assign karta hai. `DATABASE_DESIGN.md` event types ki list deta hai. `api.py::history` endpoint aur `dashboard.html` timeline dikhate hain.
code_example:
-- real, migrations/versions/0001_initial.py
CREATE TABLE history_events (       -- append-only, the single source of truth for workflow state
  workflow_id text NOT NULL REFERENCES workflows(workflow_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  event_id bigint NOT NULL,
  event_type text NOT NULL,
  attrs jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (workflow_id, event_id))
advantages: State kahin bhi rebuild ho sakta hai
Debugging: exact sequence of facts dikhta hai
disadvantages: History lagataar badhti hai -- retention chahiye
Replay cost history length ke saath badhta hai
common_mistakes: History rows ko UPDATE karna -- append-only todna replay ko corrupt karta hai
workflows.status ko source of truth samajhna; woh projection hai

question: Walk me through the event types in a workflow history, using order_processing as an example.
answer_hinglish:
flowengine mein 11 event types hain (`DATABASE_DESIGN.md`): WorkflowStarted, ActivityScheduled, ActivityCompleted, ActivityFailed, TimerStarted, TimerFired, SignalReceived, CancelRequested, WorkflowCompleted, WorkflowFailed, WorkflowCancelled.

Happy-path `order_processing` ki history aise padhte hain:
1. `WorkflowStarted {workflow_type, input, task_queue}` -- API ne `start_workflow` call kiya.
2. `ActivityScheduled {seq:1, activity_type:"reserve_inventory", args, retry}` -- pehle workflow task ne code chalaya, code ne reserve maanga.
3. `ActivityCompleted {seq:1, result:{reservation_id}}` -- activity worker ne kaam kiya.
4-5. Same for `charge_payment` (seq 2), 6-7 `ship_order` (seq 3), 8-9 `send_email` (seq 4).
10. `WorkflowCompleted {result}` -- replay mein coroutine return ho gaya.

`test_order_processing_happy_path` exactly yahi assert karta hai: pehla event WorkflowStarted, aakhri WorkflowCompleted, aur `ActivityScheduled` count == `ActivityCompleted` count == 4.

Pattern samjho: "*Scheduled / TimerStarted" events woh COMMANDS hain jo workflow code ne produce kiye (decisions); "*Completed / Failed / Fired / SignalReceived / CancelRequested" bahar ki duniya ke RESULTS hain jo workflow ko feed hote hain. Replay ke time pehli category determinism check ke liye match hoti hai, doosri futures resolve karti hai. Close events (Completed/Failed/Cancelled) pe replay loop break ho jata hai.

Retry attempts history mein events nahi banate -- woh `activity_tasks.attempt` aur `last_error` mein dikhte hain; sirf final outcome (Completed ya Failed with `attempts`) history mein aata hai.
why_needed: History padhna debugging ka pehla skill hai -- stuck workflow ho ya non-determinism, sab history se samajh aata hai.
real_world_analogy: Hospital patient chart: 'admit hua', 'test order kiya', 'test result aaya', 'doctor ne discharge kiya'. Orders aur results alag-alag entries hain, time order mein.
how_it_works: Command events `complete_workflow_task` likhta hai (workflow task ke result se); result events `complete_activity`, `fail_activity`, `fire_due_timers`, `signal`, `cancel` likhte hain -- har ek workflow row lock ke andar `_append` se.
in_this_project: Event writes: `store.py::complete_workflow_task` (ActivityScheduled/TimerStarted/Workflow*), `store.py::complete_activity`, `store.py::fail_activity`, `store.py::fire_due_timers`, `store.py::signal`, `store.py::cancel`. Reads/apply: `runtime.py::replay` ka if/elif chain. Test: `tests/test_engine.py::test_order_processing_happy_path`.
code_example:
# real, tests/test_engine.py
ev = await events_of(sm, "order-1")
assert ev[0] == "WorkflowStarted" and ev[-1] == "WorkflowCompleted"
assert ev.count("ActivityScheduled") == ev.count("ActivityCompleted") == 4

Retries history ko bloat nahi karte
disadvantages: Retry attempts ka detail history mein nahi, alag table mein dekhna padta hai
Activity args history mein plaintext JSON hain
common_mistakes: Har retry attempt ko event samajhna
TimerStarted ko timer fire hona samajhna

ActivityFailed kab likha jata hai?
Signal ka event kab aur kaise append hota hai?

question: Explain replay end to end. How does the engine rebuild a workflow's state without storing it?
answer_hinglish:
Replay ka idea: workflow function ko har workflow task pe SHURU se chalao, aur jab bhi woh kisi `ctx` future pe ruke, history se agla event feed karo. Code apne aap wahin pahunch jata hai jahan pichhli baar tha.

`runtime.py::replay` steps:
1. `WorkflowContext` banao (start time = WorkflowStarted ka created_at, RNG seed = run_id) aur coroutine ko `asyncio.ensure_future` se start karo.
2. `_settle` -- coroutine ko tab tak chalne do jab tak woh unresolved ctx futures pe block na ho jaye. Is dauran code commands produce karta hai (`ctx.commands[seq]`).
3. History events RECORDED ORDER mein: `ActivityScheduled/TimerStarted` -> check karo code ne usi seq pe same type ka command banaya (warna NonDeterminismError), seq ko `recorded` mein daalo. `ActivityCompleted/Failed/TimerFired` -> us seq ka future resolve, `SignalReceived` -> signal deliver/buffer, `CancelRequested` -> pending futures pe WorkflowCancelled; har ke baad settle again.
4. End pe: jo commands `recorded` mein nahi hain woh NEW commands hain. Coroutine done hai toh completed/failed/cancelled, warna `blocked`.
5. `finally` mein coroutine cancel -- discard. Agla task phir scratch se replay karega.

Fir `complete_workflow_task` new commands ko events + activity_tasks + timers mein badalta hai.

`test_fresh_workflow_emits_first_command_only` dikhata hai ki sirf WorkflowStarted pe code pehla command ("reserve") deta hai aur blocked rehta hai; `test_replay_continues_from_history_and_completes` mein poori history feed karo toh `completed` with result aur zero new commands.
why_needed: Replay samjhe bina determinism, non-determinism errors, performance (replay cost) -- kuch bhi explain nahi hota. Yeh project ka dil hai.
real_world_analogy: Recipe follow karna with a notebook: har baar recipe shuru se padhte ho, notebook mein dekho 'step 1 ho gaya, result yeh tha' -- skip karte jao jab tak woh step na aaye jo notebook mein nahi hai. Wahi step ab karna hai.
how_it_works: Futures bridge hain: code `await fut` karta hai, engine `_resolve(seq, result)` se fut set karta hai, event loop coroutine ko aage badhata hai. `_settle` ensure karta hai ki har event ke baad coroutine jitna aage ja sakta hai jaye, taaki commands deterministic order mein bane.
in_this_project: `flowengine/runtime.py::replay` (lines ~201-252) aur `_settle`. Caller: `worker.py::run_workflow_task_once`. Pure tests bina DB ke: `tests/test_runtime.py` (10 tests) hand-built histories pe.
code_example:
# real, flowengine/runtime.py (trimmed)
await _settle(task, ctx)
for ev in history[1:]:
    ctx._now = ev["created_at"]
    et, a = ev["event_type"], ev["attrs"]
    if et in ("ActivityScheduled", "TimerStarted"):
        ...  # determinism check against ctx.commands[a["seq"]]
        recorded.add(a["seq"]); continue
    if et == "ActivityCompleted":
        ctx._resolve(a["seq"], a.get("result"))
    ...
    await _settle(task, ctx)
new = [c for s, c in sorted(ctx.commands.items()) if s not in recorded]

disadvantages: Har task pe full replay: cost history length ke saath badhta hai (TESTING.md: 2,001 events ~102-132 ms)
Sticky cache nahi hai (README known limitation)

Replay ke dauran activity dobara chalne ki ummeed

question: Why must workflow code be deterministic, and what is forbidden inside it?
answer_hinglish:
Replay tabhi kaam karta hai jab same input + same history pe code har baar SAME commands, same order mein produce kare. Agar pehli run mein code ne seq 1 pe "reserve" maanga aur replay mein kuch aur, toh history ka `ActivityCompleted seq 1` galat jagah lag jayega -- state corrupt. Isliye workflow code deterministic hona chahiye.

Forbidden (aur replacement):
- Wall clock `datetime.now()` / `time.time()` -> `ctx.now()` (history event ka time).
- `random`, `uuid.uuid4()` -> `ctx.random()`, `ctx.uuid4()` (run_id se seeded).
- Network/DB/file I/O -> activity banao.
- `asyncio.sleep` -> `ctx.sleep` (durable timer).
- Threads, global mutable state, environment-dependent branches (config jo deploy ke beech badle) -> input ya activity result se lo.
- Unordered iteration jiska order run-to-run badal sake -> sorted use karo.

`SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` exact rules deta hai: "no wall clock, no randomness, no I/O, no threads; same inputs + same history -> same commands." `LEARNING_GUIDE.md` Step 3 isko "sabse important rule" kehta hai.

Ek doosra angle: code CHANGE bhi determinism ka issue hai. Deploy mein steps ka order badla toh purane running workflows ki history naye code se match nahi karegi -> `NonDeterminismError`. Engine isse detect karta hai (type-level), workflow ko fail nahi karta, blocked rakhta hai.

Honest gap: engine static enforcement nahi karta -- agar aapne workflow mein `datetime.now()` likha toh koi error nahi aayega, bas replays alag behave karenge.
why_needed: Determinism violations sabse common production bug hain workflow engines mein. Interviewer chahta hai aap rules aur unka reason dono bata sako.
real_world_analogy: Dance choreography ka video replay: har baar same steps same order mein. Agar dancer har baar improvise kare toh video ke subtitles (history) galat jagah lag jayenge.
how_it_works: History commands ko `seq` number se match karti hai. `seq` har `ctx.execute_activity/sleep` call pe `_next()` se badhta hai. Non-deterministic code alag order ya alag type ka command dega -> mismatch.

question: How do ctx.now(), ctx.random() and ctx.uuid4() stay deterministic across replays?
answer_hinglish:
Teeno helpers ka trick yeh hai ki unka input sirf history aur run identity se aata hai, environment se nahi.

`ctx.now()`: `WorkflowContext._now` shuru mein WorkflowStarted event ka `created_at` hai. `replay()` har event process karne se pehle `ctx._now = ev["created_at"]` set karta hai. Toh jab code kisi event ke baad aage badhta hai, `ctx.now()` us event ka recorded time return karta hai -- har replay mein bilkul same, chahe replay aaj ho ya ek mahine baad. Wall clock har replay pe alag hoti.

`ctx.random()`: `self._rng = random.Random(run_id)` -- ek private RNG jo run_id se seeded hai. Same run_id -> same sequence of numbers. Global `random` module ka state process-wide hai aur kisi bhi library se badal sakta hai, isliye woh unsafe hai.

`ctx.uuid4()`: same RNG se 128 bits leke `uuid.UUID(int=..., version=4)` banata hai. Format valid v4 UUID, lekin deterministic.

Important subtlety: yeh deterministic tabhi hain jab CALL ORDER bhi same ho. Agar replay mein code ne random() pehle 2 baar call kiya aur pichhli baar 3 baar, values shift ho jayengi. Deterministic code + deterministic helpers dono chahiye.

Test: `test_deterministic_helpers` same history ko do baar replay karta hai (`run-1`) aur `[ctx.uuid4(), ctx.random(), ctx.now().isoformat()]` dono runs mein equal assert karta hai.

Temporal mein bhi `workflow.now()`, `workflow.random()`, `workflow.uuid4()` exactly isi wajah se hain.

real_world_analogy: Seeded shuffle in a card game tournament: same seed se har table pe same card order -- dobara khelo toh same haath milenge.
how_it_works: RNG state = f(run_id, number of calls so far). Time = f(event being replayed). Dono replay-invariant hain, isliye output bhi.

question: What is a 'command' in this engine, and how are seq numbers used to match commands with history?
answer_hinglish:
Command woh request hai jo workflow code engine se karta hai -- "yeh activity schedule karo" ya "yeh timer start karo". `runtime.py` mein `Command(seq, kind, attrs)` dataclass hai; kind `schedule_activity` ya `start_timer`.

Har `ctx.execute_activity(...)` ya `ctx.sleep(...)` call `_next()` se ek naya `seq` leta hai (1, 2, 3...), `ctx.commands[seq]` mein command rakhta hai aur us seq ka future return karta hai. Toh seq = "code ne kaunse number ka command diya" -- yeh code ke execution order se deterministic aata hai.

Matching do jagah hoti hai:
1. Replay mein: history ka `ActivityScheduled {seq: 2, activity_type: "charge_payment"}` aaye toh engine `ctx.commands[2]` dekhta hai -- exist karta hai aur type same hai? Haan toh `recorded.add(2)`. Nahi toh `NonDeterminismError`.
2. Results: `ActivityCompleted {seq: 2}` -> `ctx._resolve(2, result)` -> wahi future set hota hai jo code await kar raha hai.

Replay ke end mein `new = [c for s, c in sorted(ctx.commands.items()) if s not in recorded]` -- code ne jo commands diye lekin history mein abhi nahi hain, woh naye hain. `complete_workflow_task` unhe `ActivityScheduled`/`TimerStarted` events aur `activity_tasks`/`timers` rows mein badalta hai.

seq database mein bhi key hai: `activity_tasks UNIQUE (workflow_id, seq)` aur `timers PRIMARY KEY (workflow_id, seq)` -- ek command do baar schedule ho hi nahi sakta. Aur activity idempotency key `workflow_id:seq` bhi isi se banti hai.
why_needed: seq number engine ka glue hai -- determinism check, result delivery, DB uniqueness aur idempotency keys sab isi pe tike hain.
real_world_analogy: Restaurant order tickets numbered 1, 2, 3: kitchen ticket number dekh ke plate bhejti hai, waiter number se sahi table pe deta hai. Agar waiter ne order hi alag likha toh ticket 2 ki plate galat table pe.
how_it_works: seq counter `WorkflowContext._seq` har replay mein 0 se shuru hota hai, toh deterministic code har replay mein same seq assign karta hai. Parallel activities (`asyncio.gather`) bhi deterministic order mein seq lete hain kyunki list comprehension order fixed hai.

disadvantages: Seq position-based hai: beech mein step insert kiya toh baad ke saare seq shift -- isliye versioning chahiye

question: How is non-determinism detected, what exactly is compared, and what slips through?
answer_hinglish:
Detection replay ke andar hoti hai. Jab history mein `ActivityScheduled` ya `TimerStarted` aata hai, engine `ctx.commands.get(a["seq"])` dekhta hai. Teen cases error dete hain: (1) code ne us seq pe koi command diya hi nahi, (2) history mein ActivityScheduled hai lekin code ka activity_type alag hai, (3) history mein TimerStarted hai lekin code ka command timer nahi hai. Ek aur jagah: `_resolve` -- agar history mein kisi seq ka completion hai jiska future code ne banaya hi nahi, toh bhi `NonDeterminismError`.

Kya compare NAHI hota: activity ARGUMENTS aur timer DURATION. Yeh deliberately type-level check hai, Temporal jaisa (README known limitations). Matlab agar deploy mein `notify("x", "step 1")` ko `notify("x", "step one")` kar diya, ya `ctx.sleep(60)` ko `ctx.sleep(120)`, toh detect nahi hoga. FAILURE_SCENARIOS bug #5 isi ka test-design version hai: same type ka step insert karna detect nahi hota, isliye `test_nondeterministic_deploy_is_detected_and_workflow_survives` jaan-boojh ke DIFFERENT type (`archive_document`) insert karta hai.

Detect hone ke baad: worker `stats["nondeterminism"]` badhata hai, log `workflow_nondeterminism`, aur `complete_workflow_task(wf, None, error)` workflow ko FAIL nahi karta -- `status` running rehta hai, `error` column set, `needs_task=false`. Code rollback karo, workflow resume.

Review mein mila bug (ab fixed): agar history mein ActivityScheduled hai aur naya code us seq pe TIMER deta hai, toh pehle `cmd.attrs["activity_type"]` KeyError deta tha, NonDeterminismError nahi -- worker sirf generic exception log karta, error column set nahi hota aur workflow har lease ke baad re-claim hota rehta, bina koi error dikhaye. Fix: `cmd.attrs.get("activity_type")`; regression test `test_timer_where_history_has_activity_is_nondeterminism_not_keyerror`. Blocked workflow ab fix deploy karke `POST /workflows/{id}/retry-task` se resume hota hai.
why_needed: Bad deploy production workflows tod sakta hai. Interviewer dekhna chahta hai aapko detection ki limits pata hain, sirf happy story nahi.
real_world_analogy: Exam answer-sheet checking jo sirf question number aur topic match kare, answer ka content nahi: 'Q2 - Photosynthesis' likha hai toh pass, chahe andar kuch bhi likha ho.
how_it_works: Check cost O(1) per event -- dict lookup + string compare. Args hash compare karna possible hai lekin legit changes (e.g. naya optional arg) bhi break karega; isliye type-level ek pragmatic choice hai.

question: How do signals work in this engine, including signals that arrive before the workflow waits for them?
answer_hinglish:
Signal ek external event hai jo running workflow ko data bhejta hai -- "delivery confirm hui", "manager ne approve kiya", "email verify ho gaya". Client `POST /workflows/{id}/signals/{name}` call karta hai.

Write side (`store.signal`): workflow row lock (`_lock`), status running nahi toh `Conflict` (409), warna `SignalReceived {name, payload}` event append aur `needs_task = true`. Bas -- signal history ka ek fact ban gaya, isliye durable hai.

Read side (`ctx.wait_signal(name, timeout=None)`): pehle `_signal_queues[name]` buffer check -- koi signal pehle se pada hai toh turant pop karke return. Warna ek future banao, `_signal_waiters[name]` mein daalo aur wait karo. Replay mein jab `SignalReceived` event aata hai, `ctx._signal(name, payload)` pehle waiting future dhoondhta hai; koi waiter nahi toh payload buffer queue mein append.

Buffering kyun zaroori hai: signal workflow ke wait karne se PEHLE aa sakta hai. `test_customer_onboarding_with_signal_and_durable_timer` mein `verified` signal workflow start hote hi bhej diya jata hai, jab code abhi `create_account` activity pe ruka hai. Signal history mein buffered rehta hai; jab code `wait_signal("verified")` pe pahunchta hai toh turant mil jata hai -- reminder email nahi jata (`templates == ["welcome", "tips"]`). Pure replay version: `test_signal_before_waiting_is_buffered`.

Ek limitation: `wait_signal` timeout pe `None` return karta hai, toh agar signal ka payload khud `None` ho toh dono cases distinguish nahi hote.

how_it_works: Signal = history event, isliye replay ke saath deterministic delivery. Delivery order = history order. Buffer in-memory hai lekin har replay mein history se dobara banta hai.

question: How does a durable timer work, from ctx.sleep() to TimerFired?
answer_hinglish:
Durable timer ka matlab: workflow "3 din so jao" bol sakta hai, aur beech mein saare workers restart ho jayein tab bhi 3 din baad workflow wahin se jaagega. Koi process 3 din tak memory mein wait nahi kar raha.

Flow:
1. Workflow code `await ctx.sleep(seconds)` -- yeh ek `start_timer` command banata hai (naya seq) aur future return karta hai. Replay blocked status deta hai.
2. `complete_workflow_task` command ko `TimerStarted {seq, seconds, fire_at}` event mein likhta hai aur `timers` table mein `(workflow_id, seq, fire_at)` row insert karta hai -- same transaction.
3. Ab workflow ke liye koi worker kuch nahi kar raha. CPU zero, memory zero.
4. Har worker ka `_timer_loop` har poll interval pe `store.fire_due_timers` chalata hai: `fire_at <= now()` aur `NOT fired` wale timers uthao, har ek ke liye workflow row lock, `UPDATE timers SET fired = true ... AND NOT fired`, agar row update hui aur workflow running hai toh `TimerFired {seq}` append aur `needs_task = true`.
5. Agla workflow task replay karta hai, `TimerFired` us seq ka future resolve karta hai, code aage badhta hai.

Timer `timers` table mein hai aur partial index `ix_timers_due ON timers (fire_at) WHERE NOT fired` se due timers sasta milta hai. `customer_onboarding` (`tips_after`) aur `email_campaign` (batches ke beech `pause`) iske examples hain.

Small observation: `fire_at` worker ki Python clock se compute hota hai (`datetime.now(timezone.utc)`), jabki leases DB `now()` use karte hain -- worker clocks skewed hon toh timer thoda jaldi/der se fire ho sakta hai.
why_needed: Long waits (reminders, SLA, refund windows) bina cron ke -- yeh workflow engine ka killer feature hai.
real_world_analogy: Hotel wake-up call: aap reception ko bolke so jate ho; reception ka register (timers table) yaad rakhta hai, shift badal jaye tab bhi call aayegi.
how_it_works: Timer = DB row + polling. `AND NOT fired` + workflow row lock ensure karte hain ki multiple workers ek timer ko do baar fire na karein.

Table + index in `migrations/versions/0001_initial.py`. Tests: onboarding aur campaign tests in `tests/test_engine.py`.

question: A signal and a timeout timer can both happen. How is that race resolved deterministically?
answer_hinglish:
Answer: jo event history mein PEHLE record hua woh jeetta hai, aur kyunki replay events ko recorded order mein ek-ek karke feed karta hai, har replay mein wahi jeetega.

`wait_signal(name, timeout)` andar se do futures banata hai: signal future aur `self.sleep(timeout)` timer future, phir `asyncio.wait({fut, timer}, return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)`. Real duniya mein dono events aa sakte hain -- signal API se, TimerFired timer loop se -- aur dono `_append` ke through workflow row lock ke andar likhe jaate hain, toh unhe strict event_ids milte hain. Yeh row lock hi "kaun pehle" ka referee hai.

Replay mein: agar history `TimerStarted, SignalReceived, TimerFired` hai, toh SignalReceived process hota hai, signal future resolve, `_settle` -- coroutine dekhta hai `fut in done`, return payload. Baad mein TimerFired aata hai, `_resolve` dekhta hai future already done? Nahi, timer future pending hai to resolve hota hai, lekin koi await nahi kar raha, koi effect nahi. Ulta order (`TimerFired` pehle) mein timer jeetega, None return, aur baad wala signal buffer mein chala jata hai.

`test_race_signal_first_wins` aur `test_race_timer_first_wins` exactly yahi do orders test karte hain -- same code, sirf event order badla, result "approved" vs "timed_out".

Isliye `runtime.py` docstring kehta hai: "Feeding events one at a time in their recorded order is what makes races deterministic". Agar engine saare events ek saath feed karta toh asyncio scheduling decide karta -- non-deterministic.
why_needed: Concurrency races workflow engines mein subtle bugs dete hain. Yeh question test karta hai ki aap 'total order of events' ka importance samajhte ho.
real_world_analogy: Photo finish in a race: dono runners almost saath aaye, lekin camera (row lock + event_id) ne ek order record kiya. Replay mein jitni baar video dekho, winner wahi.
how_it_works: Total order: `_append` workflow row lock ke andar `last_event_id + 1` deta hai. Deterministic delivery: `replay` loop har event ke baad `_settle` karta hai taaki coroutine ka reaction event ke turant baad compute ho.

question: How is cancellation delivered into a workflow, and how can the workflow run compensation?
answer_hinglish:
Cancellation flowengine mein "kill" nahi hai, ek MESSAGE hai jo workflow code ke andar exception ban ke pahunchta hai, taaki code cleanup/compensation chala sake.

Steps:
1. `POST /workflows/{id}/cancel {reason}` -> `store.cancel`: row lock, status running check (warna 409), `CancelRequested {reason}` append, `needs_task = true`, aur activity tasks jo `scheduled` YA `started` hain unhe `cancelled` mark. Running activity ko agla `heartbeat()` False deta hai (woh ruk sakti hai), aur uska completion fenced hai -- kabhi reap/retry nahi hoti. (Review se pehle sirf `scheduled` cancel hote the; started activity close ke baad complete hoke history mein append hoti ya reap hoke RETRY ho jaati -- fix + test `test_cancel_stops_running_activity_and_it_is_never_retried`.)
2. Agle replay mein `CancelRequested` event -> `ctx._cancel()`: `cancel_requested = True` aur us moment pe jitne PENDING futures hain (activities, timers, signal waiters) sab pe `WorkflowCancelled` exception set.
3. Workflow code jo await kar raha tha wahan `WorkflowCancelled` raise hota hai. Code `except WorkflowCancelled:` mein compensation activities schedule kar sakta hai -- yeh NAYE futures hain, aur woh normally kaam karte hain.
4. Compensation ke baad code `raise` karta hai -> replay status `cancelled` -> `WorkflowCancelled` event, status cancelled.

`document_approval` yahi karta hai: approvers ko "review cancelled" notify karke re-raise. Test `test_document_approval_escalation_and_cancellation` assert karta hai notify message mein "cancelled" hai aur last event `WorkflowCancelled`. Pure version: `test_cancellation_delivered_into_workflow_for_compensation`.

Yeh FAILURE_SCENARIOS bug #1 se seekha: pehle `_cancel` ke baad bane naye futures bhi fail ho jaate the, toh compensation kabhi chal hi nahi sakti thi. Ab `_future` comment explicitly kehta hai: sirf jo pending tha woh fail hota hai.
why_needed: Business processes cancel hote hain (order cancel, request withdraw). Bina compensation ke cancel karna = inconsistent duniya (charged but cancelled).

question: What is the saga pattern, and how does order_processing implement a long-running transaction as code?
answer_hinglish:
Saga pattern long-running distributed transaction ka tareeka hai jab ek global ACID transaction possible nahi (inventory service, payment gateway, shipping carrier -- alag systems). Har step apna local commit karta hai, aur agar baad ka step fail ho toh pehle ke steps ko COMPENSATING actions se undo karte hain (charge -> refund, reserve -> release).

`order_processing` saga ko plain code mein likhta hai:
- `reserve_inventory` -> agar `charge_payment` fail (ActivityError) toh `release_inventory`, return `payment_failed`.
- `ship_order` fail toh `refund_payment` + `release_inventory` (reverse order), return `compensated`.
- Sab theek toh `send_email` aur `completed`.

Tests effect counts se prove karte hain: card declined -> `{"reserve": 1, "release": 1}` (`test_non_retryable_failure_runs_compensation`); shipping fail -> `{"reserve": 1, "charge": 1, "refund": 1, "release": 1}` (`test_saga_compensation_when_shipping_fails`).

Sabse important point (`SYSTEM_DESIGN.md`): hand-written sagas ki sabse badi kamzori yeh hai ki agar coordinator khud compensation ke beech crash ho jaye toh compensation kabhi nahi chalti -- paise kat gaye, order cancel. Yahan workflow khud durable hai: crash ke baad doosra worker replay karke `except` block mein wahin pahunchega aur refund schedule karega. Compensation "guaranteed eventually".

Saga ACID nahi hai -- isolation nahi milti (beech mein koi charged-but-not-shipped state dekh sakta hai), aur compensations khud idempotent hone chahiye. Yahan har compensation activity bhi `workflow_id:seq` idempotency key use karti hai.
why_needed: Microservices interviews mein saga bahut puchha jata hai. 'Saga as code with durable execution' ek modern, strong answer hai.
real_world_analogy: Trip booking: flight book, hotel book, cab book. Cab nahi mili toh hotel cancel, flight cancel -- ulte order mein. Travel agent (workflow) ka notebook durable hai toh woh beech mein so bhi jaye, uthke cancellations poore karega.
how_it_works: Activity permanent fail -> `ActivityFailed` event -> replay mein `ActivityError` raise in workflow code -> except block compensation activities schedule karta hai -> normal durable flow.

question: What does RetryPolicy control, and how is the backoff delay computed?
answer_hinglish:
`RetryPolicy` decide karta hai ki fail hui activity ko kitni baar aur kitne gap ke saath dobara chalana hai. Fields (`runtime.py`):
- `initial_interval` (default 1.0s) -- pehle retry se pehle ka wait.
- `backoff_coefficient` (2.0) -- har attempt pe wait kitna guna.
- `maximum_interval` (60s) -- cap.
- `maximum_attempts` (3; 0 = unlimited).
- `non_retryable_errors` -- error type names jinko retry nahi karna.

Delay formula: `min(initial_interval * backoff_coefficient ** (attempt - 1), maximum_interval)`. Defaults pe: attempt 1 fail -> 1s, attempt 2 -> 2s, attempt 3 -> 4s ... cap 60s.

Policy workflow code mein per-activity di jaati hai (`retry=FAST`), JSON bankar `ActivityScheduled` event aur `activity_tasks.retry` column mein store hoti hai. Examples `FAST = RetryPolicy(initial_interval=0.05, maximum_interval=0.5, maximum_attempts=3)` use karte hain taaki tests jaldi chalein.

Retry kaise hota hai: `fail_activity` decide karta hai final hai ya nahi. Final nahi toh task wapas `scheduled` aur `visible_at = now() + delay` -- koi alag scheduler nahi, claim query `visible_at <= now()` filter karti hai. Final hai (non-retryable type, `NonRetryableError`, ya attempts exhausted) toh `ActivityFailed` event aur workflow ke andar `ActivityError`.

`test_retries_with_backoff_then_success_effect_once`: card "flaky" pehle 2 attempts pe ConnectionError deta hai, attempt 3 pe success; assert `attempt == 3` aur charge effect sirf 1.

Jitter: `fail_activity` actual delay `policy.delay(attempt) * random.uniform(0.8, 1.2)` rakhta hai (+-20%). Review mein yeh gap mila tha -- bina jitter ke ek shared outage mein fail hui saari activities lockstep mein retry karti. `RetryPolicy.delay` khud deterministic formula hai; jitter store layer pe lagta hai (workflow replay ko affect nahi karta kyunki retries history mein nahi jaate).
why_needed: Transient failures (network blips, rate limits) normal hain. Sahi retry policy ke bina ya toh kaam fail hota hai ya downstream pe retry storm.
real_world_analogy: Dost ko call kiya, busy aaya: 1 min baad try, phir 2 min, phir 4 min -- har baar zyada wait, aur 3 baar ke baad message chhod do. 'Number does not exist' aaye toh dobara try hi mat karo (non-retryable).
how_it_works: Retry state DB mein hai (`attempt`, `visible_at`, `last_error`), isliye worker crash ke baad bhi backoff continue. Attempt `claim_activity` mein `attempt + 1` hota hai.

Test `tests/test_engine.py::test_retries_with_backoff_then_success_effect_once`; example `FAST` in `flowengine/examples/workflows.py`.

question: Activities run at least once. How does this project get exactly-once effects?
answer_hinglish:
Pehle sach maan lo: activity ka exactly-once EXECUTION distributed system mein possible nahi. Worker ne payment gateway call ki, gateway ne charge kar diya, aur `complete_activity` likhne se pehle worker mar gaya -- engine ko nahi pata charge hua ya nahi, toh lease expire hone pe retry karega. Isliye activities at-least-once hain.

Exactly-once EFFECT ke liye idempotency chahiye: ek stable key jo us activity ke har retry aur redelivery pe SAME rahe. flowengine yeh deta hai: `ActivityContext.idempotency_key = f"{workflow_id}:{seq}"`. `seq` deterministic hai (replay mein same), aur `activity_tasks UNIQUE (workflow_id, seq)` ensure karta hai ki ek command ki ek hi task row ho. Attempt number key mein NAHI hai -- warna har retry naya key banata.

Example activities is key ko use karti hain: `effect()` helper `INSERT INTO activity_effects (idempotency_key, ...) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. Real duniya mein yahi key payment provider ko `Idempotency-Key` header ke roop mein jaati, ya business table pe unique constraint banti.

Proof tests mein: har test exact effect counts assert karta hai -- flaky card 3 attempts ke baad bhi `{"charge": 1}`; heartbeat test mein worker A mid-activity mara, B ne attempt 2 chalaya, phir bhi `{"long_task": 1}`; 2 workers x 20 workflows -> `{"reserve": 20, "charge": 20, "ship": 20, "email": 20}`.

Plus fencing: `complete_activity` `AND attempt = :a` check karta hai, toh purane attempt ka late result history mein nahi jata -- result duplicate nahi hota.
why_needed: Duplicate side effects (double charge, double email) workflow systems ka sabse costly bug hai. Interviewer 'exactly-once' claim pe hamesha push karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Bank cheque number: same cheque do baar jama karo, bank doosri baar reject karega kyunki cheque number already processed hai. Cheque number = idempotency key.
how_it_works: Two layers: (1) engine level -- unique (workflow_id, seq) + attempt fencing se ek hi result history mein; (2) effect level -- activity author key ko downstream dedupe ke liye use kare.
in_this_project: Key banana: `flowengine/worker.py::_execute` (`f"{task['workflow_id']}:{task['seq']}"`); field `flowengine/activities.py::ActivityContext`; usage `flowengine/examples/activities.py::effect`; table `activity_effects` in migration; fencing in `store.py::complete_activity`. Tests: `test_two_workers_process_many_workflows_without_duplicates`, `test_activity_heartbeat_timeout_detects_dead_worker`.

question: How is starting a workflow made idempotent, and why does it matter?
answer_hinglish:
Workflow start idempotent hai `workflow_id` pe. Client business id deta hai (jaise `order-123`), aur `workflows.workflow_id` PRIMARY KEY hai. Same id se doosri baar start karo toh naya workflow nahi banta, existing run return hota hai.

`store.start_workflow`: ek transaction mein `INSERT INTO workflows (...)` + `WorkflowStarted` append. Agar row already hai toh Postgres `IntegrityError` (PK violation) deta hai; code use catch karke existing `run_id` aur `status` padhta hai aur `{"started": False, ...}` return karta hai. Pehli call `{"started": True, run_id}`.

Kyun matter karta hai: clients retry karte hain. Checkout service ne `POST /workflows` kiya, response timeout ho gaya -- usse nahi pata workflow bana ya nahi, toh retry karega. Agar start idempotent na ho toh do order workflows -> do charges. Business id ko workflow id banana is problem ko DB constraint level pe khatam karta hai, koi alag dedupe table nahi.

Test `test_start_is_idempotent_on_workflow_id`: same id do baar start, `a["started"] and not b["started"] and a["run_id"] == b["run_id"]`.

`run_id` kya hai? Har execution ka unique uuid -- deterministic RNG ka seed bhi yahi hai. Temporal mein ek workflow_id ke kai runs ho sakte hain (continue-as-new, reuse policy); yahan simplification: ek workflow_id = ek row = ek run hamesha, closed hone ke baad bhi same id dobara start nahi ho sakta. Temporal ka 'WorkflowIdReusePolicy' yahan nahi hai.
why_needed: At-least-once clients + non-idempotent start = duplicate business processes. Yeh basic reliability hygiene hai.
real_world_analogy: Movie ticket booking mein seat number unique hai: do baar 'book seat A5' dabao, doosri baar system kehta hai 'already booked by you', naya ticket nahi.
how_it_works: Unique constraint as dedupe: DB atomically decide karta hai kaun pehla tha. Loser path sirf read karta hai.

question: Describe Temporal's architecture and map flowengine onto it. Where does flowengine simplify?
answer_hinglish:
Temporal cluster ke main parts: Frontend service (API gateway: start, signal, query), History service (har workflow ki event history aur mutable state own karta hai; workflows `workflow_id` hash se history SHARDS mein bante hain, har shard ek history host ke paas), Matching service (task queues: workflow tasks aur activity tasks workers tak deliver, long-poll), persistence (Cassandra/Postgres/MySQL), aur Workers jo aapke process mein SDK ke saath chalte hain -- workflow tasks replay karte hain, activity tasks execute karte hain. Server aapka code kabhi nahi chalata.

flowengine mapping:
- Frontend -> `api.py` (FastAPI): start, signal, cancel, describe, history, replay-check.
- History service -> `store.py` + `history_events` table: `_append` row lock ke andar, `complete_workflow_task` commands ko events mein badalta hai.
- Matching service -> koi alag service nahi; Postgres tables hi task queues hain: workflow tasks = `workflows.needs_task`, activity tasks = `activity_tasks`, dono SKIP LOCKED se claim.
- Timer queue -> `timers` table + `fire_due_timers`.
- Workers -> `worker.py`: workflow-task poller, activity poller, timer+reaper loop, heartbeat.

Simplifications (README + SYSTEM_DESIGN): single Postgres (no history shards); polling instead of long-poll push; full replay har task pe (no sticky cache); no continue-as-new; no versioning API; no child workflows/queries/schedules; no namespaces/auth; timers aur reaper har worker mein (Temporal mein server-side).

Core ideas same hain: event history as truth, workflow vs activity tasks, determinism, task queues, stateless workers.
why_needed: Interviewer check karta hai ki aapne Temporal ka concept samajh ke banaya ya bas naam liya. Mapping + honest simplifications credibility dete hain.
real_world_analogy: Big hospital vs clinic: hospital mein reception, records department, scheduling desk alag departments hain; clinic mein ek register aur ek receptionist sab karta hai. Kaam same, scale alag.
how_it_works: Temporal server state machine + queues manage karta hai, SDK workers deterministic code chalate hain. flowengine mein 'server' logic store functions mein hai jo workers aur API dono call karte hain -- shared database hi coordination point.

question: Walk through the lifecycle of one workflow step: how do workflow tasks and activity tasks flow through the system?
answer_hinglish:
Do tarah ke tasks hain. Workflow task = "is workflow ko replay karo aur decide karo aage kya". Activity task = "yeh side-effect wala kaam karo". `ARCHITECTURE.md` ka sequence diagram yahi hai:

1. API: `start_workflow` -> `WorkflowStarted` event, `needs_task = true` (column default).
2. Workflow worker: `claim_workflow_task` -> lease lo (SKIP LOCKED), history 1..N padho (N = last_event_id) -- transaction khatam.
3. Replay transaction ke BAHAR (pure CPU): code ne activity "charge" maangi (seq 2).
4. Commit (`complete_workflow_task`): row lock, `last_event_id` abhi bhi N? Haan toh `ActivityScheduled(seq 2)` append, `activity_tasks` row insert (status scheduled), `needs_task = false`, lease clear. Ek transaction.
5. Activity worker: `claim_activity` -> status started, attempt+1, lease. Activity chalti hai idempotency key `wf:2` ke saath.
6. `complete_activity`: workflow row lock, fenced update (attempt match), `ActivityCompleted(seq 2, result)` append, `needs_task = true`.
7. Workflow worker phir claim karta hai, replay 1..N+2: seq 2 resolve, code aage badhta hai, next command ya completion.

Key design: workflow tasks decisions karte hain aur kabhi I/O nahi; activity tasks I/O karte hain aur kabhi decisions nahi. Dono ke beech communication sirf history events + `needs_task` flag se. Timers aur signals bhi bas events append karke `needs_task = true` set karte hain -- "workflow ko jagao".

Ek worker process dono roles karta hai (`Worker.run` dono loops start karta hai), lekin task_queue/type filters se specialize kar sakte ho.
why_needed: Yeh end-to-end flow interview whiteboard ka centerpiece hai -- isse har component ka role aur har transaction boundary clear hoti hai.
real_world_analogy: Manager (workflow task) aur employee (activity task): manager file padh ke decide karta hai 'charge karo', task board pe card lagata hai. Employee card uthata hai, kaam karke file mein result likhta hai aur manager ki inbox mein flag lagata hai.
how_it_works: needs_task = workflow task queue; activity_tasks = activity queue; history = shared memory. Har transition ek short transaction with workflow row lock -- events ka total order.

    if wf is None:

question: Why are workers stateless here, and how can any worker continue any workflow?
answer_hinglish:
Worker ke paas koi workflow-specific state nahi hoti jo crash pe kho jaye. Saari state do jagah hai: workflow CODE (har worker process mein registered same code -- `WORKFLOWS`, `ACTIVITIES`) aur HISTORY (Postgres). Workflow state = replay(code, history). Isliye koi bhi worker, kabhi bhi, kisi bhi workflow ka next task utha sakta hai.

`worker.py` docstring: "Workers are stateless -- any worker can continue any workflow from its history." `run_workflow_task_once` har baar history DB se padhta hai aur `replay` ke `finally` mein coroutine cancel kar deta hai -- next task scratch se. Activity side bhi stateless: task row mein input, retry policy, attempt sab hai.

Is design se teen cheezein free milti hain:
1. Crash recovery: `test_worker_crash_another_worker_resumes_from_history` -- worker A onboarding ko timer tak le gaya aur gaya; worker B (fresh) ne complete kiya, har effect exactly once.
2. Horizontal scaling: workers count se scale (`docker compose up -d --scale worker=4`), koi affinity/sticky routing nahi.
3. Easy deploys: rolling restart safe -- graceful stop current task finish karta hai, baaki doosre workers uthate hain.

Leases is model ka safety net hain: worker claim karte waqt `lease_until` set karta hai; mar gaya toh lease expire hone pe doosra worker claim kar sakta hai.

Cost: stateless = har task full replay. Temporal 'sticky execution' se optimize karta hai -- last worker ke paas workflow state cache rehta hai, cache miss pe hi full replay. flowengine mein yeh nahi hai (README known limitation), aur replay cost measured hai: 2,001 events pe ~102-132 ms.
why_needed: Stateless workers distributed systems ka classic pattern hai; interviewer dekhna chahta hai aap jaante ho state 'kahan' gayi aur iski kya keemat hai.
real_world_analogy: Call center agents: koi bhi agent aapki call utha sakta hai kyunki poori complaint history CRM mein hai, agent ke dimaag mein nahi.
how_it_works: Code everywhere + history in DB + leases for ownership. Ownership temporary hai (lease), state permanent hai (history).

Scaling `DEPLOYMENT.md` rule 2 ('Workers are stateless: scale by count'). Test `tests/test_engine.py::test_worker_crash_another_worker_resumes_from_history`.
